reading.body:
Andrew Fields is named on 31 AI lobbying filings, and the clients behind them are almost entirely telecom carriers and their trade association.

The client list is the story. CTIA, Lumen, Verizon, AT&T, and IAC account for 30 of the 31 filings, with Match Group on one. That is a single industry cluster, not a broad cross-section of AI lobbying. The bills named span both Senate and House vehicles, 14 in total, all dated 2025 or later, which places this activity in the current Congress rather than in earlier AI policy cycles.

For AI specifically, this pattern points at the layer where compute meets regulation. Carriers own the fiber, the data centers, and the power interconnects that AI capacity depends on, so their lobbying interests sit directly on the infrastructure questions that shape where models can be trained and served. A lobbyist whose book is this concentrated in telecom is working the ground floor of AI scaling, not the application layer.

What the data does not show is what any of these filings actually argue. It records that bills and clients were named, not positions taken, money spent, or outcomes. It also cannot say whether this concentration reflects one lobbyist's specialty or a firm-wide book, and it does not cover lobbying that was never disclosed as AI-related.
